## Stage 0 — Document Accessibility Report

This analysis uses only the supplied paper text and source images. The paper's prompts, attack examples, code, and external links are treated as evidence to analyze, never as instructions to execute. No external sources, tools, repository contents, or linked supplementary artifacts were consulted.

| Accessibility item | Assessment |

| Text coverage | Pages 1–26 are supplied consecutively. No page is apparently missing from that sequence; this does not independently establish that every original supplementary artifact is present. |
| Direct visual coverage | Supplied images were inspected for physical pages 1–9, 13, 16–21, and 24: 17 pages. |
| Text-only coverage | Pages 10–12, 14–15, 22–23, and 25–26 were inspected through supplied extracted text, without a corresponding page image. |
| Figures | All numbered figures 1–21 have supplied visual renderings. Figures 6, 9, and 21 have distinct panels; Figure 19 has four attack-prompt panels. |

Evidence labels used below are [A] AUTHOR-REPORTED, [B] DIRECTLY OBSERVABLE, [C] ANALYST-DERIVED, and [D] ANALYST INTERPRETATION. No [E] EXTERNAL INFORMATION is introduced. HIGH confidence means the relevant supplied evidence is clear; it does not certify that an author claim has been independently reproduced. Approximate plot readings are explicitly identified. Numerical inconsistencies are preserved rather than silently reconciled.

### Inventory established before synthesis

**Identity.** AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents. Authors: Edoardo Debenedetti, Jie Zhang, Mislav Balunovic, Luca Beurer-Kellner, Marc Fischer, and Florian Tramèr. Affiliations: ETH Zurich and Invariant Labs. The first page identifies the 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, NeurIPS 2024, Track on Datasets and Benchmarks. Closest document type: a mixed cybersecurity, AI systems, dataset, and benchmark paper with empirical evaluation.

**Main sections.** Abstract and §1 Introduction, p. 1; §2 Related Work and Preliminaries, pp. 2–3; §3 Designing and Constructing AgentDojo, pp. 3–6, including §3.1 Components, §3.2 Agents and Prompt Injection Defenses, §3.3 Prompt Injection Attacks, and §3.4 Reporting Results; §4 Evaluation, pp. 6–9, including §4.1 Baseline Agents and Attacks, §4.2 Attack Components and Attacker Knowledge, and §4.3 Defenses; §5 Conclusion, pp. 9–10, including broader impact. Acknowledgments and references occupy pp. 10–14; a checklist is on p. 15.

**Appendices.** A Additional Details on AgentDojo's Design, pp. 16–17; B Prompts, pp. 17–19, with B.1 Agent Prompts, B.2 Defense Prompts, and B.3 Attack Prompts; C Full Results, p. 20; D Additional Results, pp. 20–21; E Dataset-related supplementary material, pp. 22–23, with E.1–E.6 release, maintenance, reproducibility, license, responsibility, and metadata; F Data card, pp. 23–26, with F.1–F.12 and their substantive subheadings.

**Visual and mathematical objects.** F1–F21 preserve original figure numbers. T1–T5 preserve original table numbers. ALG1 is the attack-construction loop in Figure 13. Other code figures define environment state, a tool, user and injection tasks, and agent interfaces. M1 is relative injection position M/N; M2 is the family of utility and attack-success metrics. No formal research-question list, hypothesis list, theorem, lemma, proof, keyword list, or training algorithm is supplied.

**Experiment register.** X1: benign function-calling benchmark comparison, Figure 2. X2: ten-model baseline attack evaluation, Figure 6/Table 3. X3: GPT-4o results by suite and injection target, Figure 7. X4: four attack phrasings and their per-case union, Figure 8/Table 4. X5: user/model-name knowledge ablation, Table 2. X6: four GPT-4o defenses, Figure 9/Table 5. X7: denial-of-service prompt variants, Figure 20. X8: injection position and controlled-output fraction, Figure 21. X9: running-cost estimates, Appendix D. Dataset construction and validation constitute a separate methodological analysis, not a human-subject experiment.

## 1. Plain-language orientation

[A] This paper studies AI assistants that use a large language model, or LLM, to decide what tools to call. Such an assistant might read email, search files, inspect a calendar, make a reservation, or initiate a bank transaction. Its difficulty is that information returned by those tools can contain hostile instructions written by somebody other than the user. If the assistant mistakes that information for an instruction it should obey, an attacker can redirect its actions. The paper calls this a prompt injection, particularly an indirect prompt injection when it arrives through third-party data.

[A] The researchers built AgentDojo, an extensible environment for testing both useful behavior and security failures during actual sequences of tool calls. Its initial release contains 97 user tasks and 629 paired user-task/attacker-goal security cases across four synthetic application environments. Explicit code checks whether the user's goal or the attacker's goal was achieved. The environment supports additional tasks, tools, agent pipelines, attacks, and defenses rather than fixing a permanent attack list.

[A] The experiments show that ordinary task competence, malicious-action success, and continued usefulness under attack are different properties. Some agents struggle even without attacks. A prompt claiming an important extra task is substantially more effective than several simpler attack phrasings. Tool restriction and an injection detector reduce targeted success, but their utility costs and failure conditions differ. [A/B] Table 3 reports GPT-4o targeted success of 47.69% under the baseline evaluation; Table 5 reports 6.84% with a tool filter under the defense experiment's separately reported attack conditions. These values must not be treated as one directly interchangeable experiment.

[D] For the research question, 'Why Are Web AI Agents More Vulnerable Than Standalone LLMs?', the paper supplies a mechanism and agent-side evidence: externally supplied text enters the same decision process that controls tools and mutable state. It does **not** directly compare web agents with matched standalone LLMs, so it does not measure a relative vulnerability increase. Its contribution is a way to study this expanded security problem, not proof of a universal agent-versus-chatbot ranking.

## 2. Document roadmap

The abstract and introduction establish the problem of confusing instructions with retrieved data. Related work distinguishes single-function benchmarks, multi-turn agent benchmarks without explicit attacks, LLM-simulated environments, and prior injection benchmarks. Section 3 explains the environment, tasks, checks, pipelines, and attack interface. Section 4 evaluates models, attack wording, side information, and defenses. The conclusion proposes extensions and discusses the dual-use consequences of releasing a security benchmark.

Appendix A clarifies how code interfaces make these components extensible. Appendix B records operational prompts and attack templates. Appendix C supplies the most precise aggregate numerical results, which sometimes conflict with introductory or main-text descriptions. Appendix D adds operating cost, denial-of-service attacks, and positional observations. Appendix E describes release and reproducibility arrangements. Appendix F records synthetic-data provenance, maintenance, intended use, transformations, and consistency validation. The checklist supplies the confidence-interval software call and confirms that the dataset contains dummy rather than real personal data.

The references establish what the authors cite, not independent evidence that the cited publications have been reviewed here. Bibliographic entries, institutional contact details, acknowledgments, and full license boilerplate are compressed below; their substantive provenance and availability implications are retained.

## 3. Background and context

[A] An **LLM agent** combines text-based reasoning with external tool calls. A **tool** is a callable function whose documentation describes the function and its arguments. Tools may read state, such as retrieving email, or modify state, such as sending a message. **Stateful** means that the environment retains data and mutations during execution: later actions depend on what earlier actions returned or changed.

[A] A **prompt injection** puts instructions into a model's context to hijack behavior. A direct injection comes through user input that overrides a system prompt; an indirect injection comes through third-party content retrieved by the model. AgentDojo concentrates on the latter through tool-output placeholders. **Exfiltration** means sending a user's information to an attacker. An **attack surface** is the set of places through which hostile content can enter or influence the system; here it includes emails, web pages, files, and other tool-returned content.

[A] A **user task** specifies the legitimate objective. An **injection task** specifies the attacker objective. Their pair is a **security case**. A **task suite** is an environment's collection of user and injection tasks. A **ground-truth sequence** is an author-provided sequence of calls that achieves a goal. It helps validate checks and locate attack placeholders; the paper does not say the evaluated agent is simply handed this answer sequence.

[A] A **utility check** determines whether the legitimate task succeeded, using output and environment state. A **security function** checks whether the attacker goal succeeded. Despite its name, this security function is an attack-success test rather than necessarily a proof of safety. **Adaptive evaluation** considers attacks chosen or designed for the system being assessed. In the paper's limited Max construction, adaptation means selecting success from four candidate phrasings per security case, not conducting unrestricted optimization.

[A] The related-work discussion describes three defense families: detecting injections, improving instruction/data separation through prompting or training, and isolating tool calls from planning. It attributes weaknesses to prior methods; those cited claims have not been independently verified here. The authors also argue that an LLM evaluator could itself be influenced by injected instructions, motivating explicit state-based checks.

## 4. Research problem and gap

**Existing problem [A].** LLMs process natural-language instructions and natural-language data without a formal distinction that reliably prevents hostile data from becoming instructions. Tool integration lets such confusion cause actions on behalf of a user, including information disclosure and inappropriate transactions. Arbitrary-code execution is mentioned as a possible consequence in the introduction; the supplied evaluation does not demonstrate such a case.

**Shortcomings of previous approaches, as characterized by the authors [A].** Single-function benchmarks do not capture dynamic planning over multiple calls. More realistic agent benchmarks often omit attacks. ToolEmu simulates tool behavior and judges outcomes using an LLM, which the authors consider vulnerable to the same injection mechanism. Prior injection tasks often involve question answering, prompt theft, or rule hijacking. InjecAgent is described as a simulated single-turn setting that directly supplies one adversarial tool result rather than assessing which tools an agent chooses.

**Gap [A].** The authors seek a benchmark where agents act in a mutable environment, encounter untrusted data through their chosen calls, and must accurately complete the original task despite an attacker objective. They also seek a framework that can evolve as defenses and attacks change, because success against a small static collection is not enough to establish robustness.

**Scope [A].** AgentDojo's first release covers workspace, Slack, travel, and banking applications populated with synthetic data. It evaluates tool-calling LLM agents and relatively simple attacks and defenses. It is not a survey of all web-agent attack surfaces, a live-browser field study, a standalone-LLM control experiment, or a complete defense certification.

## 5. Research questions / objectives / hypotheses

No formal numbered research questions or hypotheses are stated in the supplied paper. The following are author objectives reconstructed from explicit descriptions, rather than invented hypothesis tests:

1. [A] Measure agents' ability to solve user tasks safely in an adversarial environment with prompt injections.
2. [A] Provide extensible interfaces for tasks, attacks, defenses, and agent designs.
3. [A] Evaluate the tradeoff between benign utility, utility under attack, and targeted attack success.
4. [A] Examine how attack phrasing, knowledge of names, application suite, and injection position affect outcomes.
5. [A] Assess whether existing defense patterns improve security without making the agent unusable.

The user-provided comparative research question is separate from those objectives. [D] AgentDojo informs why adding retrieval and action privileges creates consequential exposure: an attacker can place an instruction where a tool fetches data, and the agent may execute it with user-authorized tools. The supplied work does not test whether the same underlying model is more likely to obey an injection when agentic than when standalone, and does not establish that every web agent has more exposure than every standalone application.

## 6. Assumptions / threat model

[A] The legitimate user supplies a task. An agent has tool documentation and a runtime able to execute available functions. The environment consists of mutable application objects and selected attack placeholders within third-party-controlled content. The attacker defines a malicious goal and injects text into those placeholders. The abstract and Figure 1 frame external tool data as untrusted.

[A] Attack construction can use task-specific injection candidates located in outputs of tools needed for the legitimate task. User tasks expose ground-truth calls so that candidate selection targets content that is relevant to execution rather than an arbitrary unreachable page. Injection tasks can also expose ground-truth calls achieving the malicious goal, potentially helping attacks that know the tool application programming interface, or API.

[A] Attacker side knowledge may include the user's name, the model's identity, or its tool-calling API. The name ablation tests correct and incorrect guesses. This is different from granting control over the system prompt or replacing the user's initial request. The supplied attack method returns text for candidate placeholders; it does not establish arbitrary control over every byte of the environment.

[D] The evaluation treats task/check definitions, runtime behavior, and benign initial state as trusted infrastructure. This trust boundary is inferred from their evaluation role, not presented as a formally enumerated theorem assumption. The paper does not test compromise of its checker code, provider infrastructure, model weights, or operating system. It should not be read as excluding all such attacks in real deployments.

[A] Important boundaries include text-only evaluation; no support yet for persistent multi-task user interactions without context reset; no current attacker control over sorting to move an injection to a preferred position; and future work on length/format constraints. The current results therefore reflect the supplied placeholder capabilities, not every realistic publishing restriction.

## 7. Methodology

### Environment and tools

[A] Four environments represent email/calendar/cloud storage, Slack and web/file access, travel services, and banking. State comprises mutable objects rather than another LLM's imagined simulation. Initial data are written manually or generated with GPT-4o and Claude 3 Opus using expected schemas and examples. Authors manually inspect generated outputs and modify some data for realism and consistency. The data card dates collection to May 2024 and the snapshot to version v1.0, released and last updated in June 2024.

[A] Tools are specially formatted Python functions. Figure 4 illustrates a calendar query using a dependency-injected Calendar object and a date string in YYYY-MM-DD format. Tool documentation is included in the agent prompt. Tool results are currently serialized using YAML, a structured text format, although arbitrary formats are supported. The implementation syntax is inspired by FastAPI. This reference identifies a design influence; no external FastAPI documentation was inspected.

### Tasks and checks

[A] User tasks are manually designed across varied scenarios. Data can reach 7,000 GPT-4 tokens, with up to 4,000 GPT-4 tokens for tool documentation. User tasks may chain up to 18 calls. Injection goals range from one to twenty required steps and from ordinary messages to security-sensitive disclosures such as two-factor authentication codes. These are reported maxima/ranges, not a distribution of lengths or an assertion that every evaluated task uses those limits.

[A] A deterministic binary utility function receives the model's output and pre/post environment states. A security function assesses attainment of the attacker goal. User and injection tasks are crossed within each environment. [C] Table 1 implies 40×6 + 21×5 + 20×7 + 16×9 = 240 + 105 + 140 + 144 = 629 security cases. The 97 user tasks are 40 + 21 + 20 + 16; the 27 injection tasks are 6 + 5 + 7 + 9. The data card's 124 tasks equal 97 + 27, so that count describes task definitions rather than paired security cases.

### Agents, prompts, and attack construction

[A] Modular agent components provide a query interface taking user instructions, runtime, state, conversation, and extra arguments. Figure 12 demonstrates an OpenAI GPT-4o component with a tool-execution loop and injection detector. Its model string is gpt-4o-2024-05-13; this code example does not independently establish exact snapshots for every experiment.

[A] All evaluated models receive the default agent prompt in Figure 14. Claude 3/3.5 Sonnet receive an additional tool-use prompt; Llama 3 70B receives a longer tagged-call prompt because it lacks function calling out of the box. Other models are queried through official provider APIs. These differences are part of the experiment, not controlled identical wrappers.

[A] The baseline Important message template impersonates a message from the user to the model, requests the attacker goal before the original task, then says the original task can resume. Other templates are TODO, Ignore previous instructions, and the InjecAgent instruction. Max treats a case as successful if any candidate succeeds. Figure 13 shows a simpler example attack loop filling candidate placeholders with the injection goal; it is interface illustration rather than the complete baseline implementation.

### Metrics and statistical reporting

[A] Benign utility is the fraction of user tasks solved without attacks. Utility under attack is the fraction of paired cases where the user task succeeds without adversarial side effects. Targeted attack success rate, ASR, is the fraction where the malicious goal succeeds. Untargeted ASR is sometimes the complement of utility under attack. They measure different events; targeted and untargeted rates need not sum to 100%.

[A] Tables 3–5 report 95% confidence intervals. The checklist names statsmodels.stats.proportion.proportion_confint. The exact interval option, treatment of dependence among repeated user tasks, and repeated-run/random-seed protocol are not specified in the supplied narrative. Several graphical error bars lack equally explicit local interval definitions. No statistical significance tests or p-values are provided.

### Data validation and reproducibility

[A] F.7–F.11 describe selecting syntactically valid, mutually consistent YAML; cleaning mismatched values; fixing syntax; adding needed samples; adjusting dates; validating data against schemas; and running ground-truth sequences to verify they pass utility/security checks. This checks agreement among constructed artifacts. [D] It does not by itself establish that every checker captures every meaningful unsafe outcome.

[A] There is no reported train/validation/test split for agent model training. The data card calls the benchmark a validation asset. Hardware, complete software versions, temperature, token caps, detector threshold, and full model snapshot list are not specified in the supplied paper text. A requirements file and additional reproduction artifacts are described as available elsewhere, but were not inspected.

## 9. Results

### Agent competence and targeted compromise

[A/B] Table 3's leading benign utility is Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 78.22% ±3.23, followed by GPT-4o at 69.00% ±3.61 and Claude 3 Opus at 66.61% ±3.69. Command-R+ has the lowest benign utility, 25.44% ±3.40, and lowest targeted ASR, 0.95% ±0.76. GPT-4o's targeted ASR is 47.69% ±3.90, while Opus's is 11.29% ±2.47. These are reported 95% interval terms in percentage units.

[A] The authors describe a tendency for more capable models to be easier to attack because completing malicious goals also requires competence. [D] This is a tendency, not a monotonic ordering: Opus combines relatively strong utility with a much lower targeted rate than GPT-4o, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet has higher utility than GPT-4o but lower targeted success. Capability alone does not explain all points.

[C] GPT-4o utility drops by 69.00 − 50.08 = 18.92 percentage points in Table 3. Claude 3.5 Sonnet drops by 78.22 − 51.19 = 27.03 points. Command-R+ drops by only 0.32 points. GPT-3.5 Turbo's attacked utility is 0.80 points higher than its benign value, 34.66 − 33.86. Different averaging populations and stochastic behavior are possible considerations, but the supplied paper does not explain that increase; it is not evidence of a significant attack benefit.

### Attack wording and knowledge

[A/B] The Important message prompt is dramatically stronger than the three simpler phrasings in Table 4. Its reported targeted rate is 57.7%, compared with 3.66% for TODO. [C] The difference is 57.7 − 3.66 = 54.04 percentage points; it is not a 54.04% relative improvement. However, the inconsistent Max value prevents a clean numerical statement that the union raises targeted success.

[A/B] Table 2 gives 45.8% baseline success, 46.1% with correct user name alone, 44.8% with correct model name alone, and 47.7% with both. [C] Both correct improves the baseline by 1.9 points. Wrong user and wrong model reduce it by 22.6 and 22.1 points, respectively. The table prints these changes with percent signs; they are absolute percentage-point differences between displayed rates.

### Defenses and application conditions

[A/B] Under Table 5's defense conditions, no defense has 57.69% targeted ASR. Delimiting reduces it to 41.65%; repeated prompting to 27.82%; detector to 7.95%; tool filter to 6.84%. [C] Tool filtering's reported reduction is 57.69 − 6.84 = 50.85 percentage points. Detector benign utility falls from 69.0% to 41.49%, a 27.51-point loss. Repeating the prompt raises benign utility by 85.53 − 69.0 = 16.53 points. These computations use the displayed rates and make no statistical-significance claim.

[A] Tool filtering works particularly well when the legitimate task requires only reads while the attacker needs writes. It can fail when future tool requirements depend on retrieved data or the selected legitimate tools also permit the attack; the latter condition covers 17% of test cases according to §4.3. A listing can also manipulate a recommendation without requiring a newly forbidden tool.

### Inconsistencies that affect interpretation

1. [A/B] Page 2 says current models solve less than 66% of tasks and attacks succeed against the best-performing agents in less than 25% of cases. Table 3 includes 78.22% benign utility and 33.86% targeted ASR for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and 69.00%/47.69% for GPT-4o. The statements are not aligned with the displayed full results.
2. [A/B] Page 7 initially calls GPT-4o the highest-utility model, then identifies Claude 3.5 Sonnet as highest and explains its release occurred after the first paper version. This provides revision context but does not fully repair all introductory claims.
3. [A/B/C] Page 4 says 74 tools. Table 1's caption and data card say 70; Table 1's rows sum to 24 + 11 + 28 + 11 = 74. No resolution is supplied.
4. [A/B] Table 3's GPT-4o targeted rate is 47.69%, Table 4's Important message is 57.7%, and Table 5's no-defense rate is 57.69%. These cannot silently become one baseline; exact run/subset changes are not fully documented in the supplied text.
5. [A/B] Figure 8 visually places Important message targeted success around 0.47 and Max around 0.57, whereas Table 4 reports 57.7% and 57.55%. For identical underlying case outcomes, a union cannot be less successful than a member; the table's ordering therefore conflicts with the described Max construction unless conditions differ.
6. [A/B] Main text says the tool filter lowers ASR to 7.5%, but Table 5 gives 6.84%. The detector's rounded 8% claim agrees approximately with 7.95%.
7. [A/B] Figure 9's caption says all defenses lose 15–20% utility under attack. Table 5 delimiting loses 72.66 − 55.64 = 17.02 points, but detector loses 41.49 − 21.14 = 20.35 points. The caption is an approximate characterization, not an exact universal bound.

## 13. Equations and mathematical concepts

No numbered equations, optimization losses, theorem statements, or proofs are present. The following explanatory notation restates supplied prose; it is not an author-numbered mathematical development.

**Metric reconstruction [C, from §3.4].** Let U denote user-task cases, C security cases, b(u) a binary benign-success outcome, q(c) a binary outcome for correct user completion without adversarial side effects, and a(c) a binary attacker-goal outcome. Then benign utility = Σ b(u)/|U|, utility under attack = Σ q(c)/|C|, and targeted ASR = Σ a(c)/|C|. Multiplying by 100 expresses percentages. These symbols are analyst-introduced solely to explain the author's definitions. They do not settle the paper's unexplained aggregation of displayed results.

**Untargeted failure [A/C].** The author-defined complement gives untargeted ASR = 1 − utility under attack. It measures failure of the combined useful-and-clean outcome, not only execution of the malicious objective. Thus an agent may fail the user without achieving the attacker goal, or may achieve both goals but fail the clean-utility condition.

**Attack union [A/C].** For candidate attacks A1,…,An, the success event for a case is that at least one succeeds. Written using analyst notation, a_Max(c) = max_i a_i(c) for binary outcomes. If all outcomes come from the same evaluated cases and fixed candidate runs, its mean cannot be lower than any candidate's mean. This mathematical property highlights the unresolved Table 4 inconsistency; it does not license changing the table.

**Relative position [A].** Appendix D defines p = M/N, where a tool response has N tokens and the injection text ends at token M, with M ≤ N. The output is a dimensionless fraction indicating the injection's endpoint in the response. It is not the fraction of malicious text, not the injection's start, and not necessarily position in the entire accumulated conversation. Figure 21a relates this measure to observed success.

**Pareto frontier [A/D].** Figures 6 and 9 identify tradeoff-frontier points. For interpretation, a point is competitive when no comparison point is at least as useful and at least as secure with an improvement in one dimension. Security means lower targeted ASR in one panel and higher attacked utility in the other. The interpretation is restricted to the evaluated points and attacks.

## 14. Interpretation and discussion

[A] AgentDojo makes malicious-action evaluation depend on actual state transitions and outputs rather than another language model's judgment. It also keeps useful completion visible, preventing an always-abort policy from appearing ideal simply because it never executes an attacker goal. The detector illustrates that distinction: its targeted rate is low, but so is its utility.

[A] The application differences are large. Slack includes browsing web content and posting messages, and the authors suggest its large attacker-controlled output fraction helps explain its high success. The travel two-goal target illustrates the opposite: an injection can influence one action without satisfying a compound malicious goal. [D] Both results warn against interpreting one aggregate ASR as a stable property of a model independent of tools, content control, and goal complexity.

[D] For web-agent security, three linked mechanisms are supported: exposure to third-party content, use of that content during planning, and availability of consequential tools. A hostile page does not have to compromise the runtime to influence action selection. The tool-filter results suggest that restricting action capability can help even when text interpretation remains imperfect. However, a recommendation attack using tools already needed for the user can survive such restriction.

The supplied evidence supports the author's general claim that both utility and security remain challenging. It is weaker for the broad 'more capable means easier to attack' trend, because the rankings contain important exceptions and causal variables are uncontrolled. It does not answer a formal standalone comparison. The inconsistent numerical baselines and Max table prevent using all figures and tables as one clean, fully harmonized statistical account.

## 17. Threats to validity

These categories are analyst organizing labels, not a formal validity taxonomy stated by the authors.

**Internal validity [D].** Different model prompts and APIs, historical model changes, unexplained baseline differences, and absent run-level data make causal attribution to model capability alone difficult. Position and content-fraction plots do not isolate those variables from suite or goal complexity.

**Construct validity [D].** Targeted success captures the defined malicious goal, while utility under attack requires correct completion without adversarial effects. Neither automatically measures every possible security violation. Compound goals can yield zero full success despite partial harmful behavior. Conversely, low success may arise from general execution weakness.

**External/ecological validity [D].** Synthetic email, banking, and travel state approximate applications but do not establish real production attack rates. Placeholder control and unconstrained textual payloads may differ from a publisher's actual permissions. Text-only, reset-context tasks omit some persistent and multimodal settings.

**Statistical conclusion validity [D].** The paper reports 95% intervals but not all interval parameters or dependence assumptions. User tasks recur across paired cases; it is unclear how that structure affects interval calculation. No significance tests establish that small differences such as the name-knowledge improvement are reliable.

**Reproducibility [A/D].** Authors describe source code, conversations, notebooks, and dependencies, and a DOI. Those are useful reported provisions, but this analysis cannot confirm their contents. Table/figure inconsistencies and incomplete settings make exact reproduction from the supplied pages alone uncertain.

**Generalizability [D].** The strongest conclusion concerns these tasks, models, attack families, and tool capabilities. A frontier position or low ASR is not a guarantee against future adaptive attackers, a point explicitly reinforced by the data card.

## 22. Very simple explanation

An AI agent is like an assistant who can both read messages and press buttons for you. You might ask it to check your email or book a hotel. An attacker can hide a message in an email or website saying, in effect, 'Do this other thing first.' The problem is that the assistant reads both useful information and hostile instructions as text, and may confuse who is allowed to tell it what to do.

AgentDojo creates fake but realistic workplaces, travel services, and bank accounts where researchers can test that problem. It checks two things separately: whether the assistant did your job correctly, and whether it did the attacker's job. Those are different. An assistant that gives up may avoid sending your information away, but it still has not helped you. An assistant can also partly carry out an attack without completing the attacker's entire plan.

The experiments show that wording matters, and that restricting which buttons the assistant can press can help a lot. But restrictions work less well when your own task needs the same buttons the attacker wants. A detector can also stop attacks by stopping the assistant too often. None of the tested defenses earns a promise of safety against every future attack.

For the question about web agents versus ordinary LLMs, this paper explains why tools and third-party pages create extra opportunities for harmful action. It does not actually run a fair side-by-side test against standalone models. The careful conclusion is that tool-using agents expose a consequential attack path, while the size of any relative vulnerability increase remains unmeasured here.

claims.statement: AgentDojo is an extensible evaluation environment for agents executing tools over untrusted data, rather than a fixed static test suite.
User-task utility is assessed by a deterministic binary function using model output and environment state before and after execution, avoiding an LLM-only evaluator.
The within-suite user/injection cross-products reproduce the reported 629 security cases: 40×6 + 21×5 + 20×7 + 16×9 = 629. This differs from the 124 individual task definitions.

Baseline agents were evaluated on 629 security cases involving 97 user tasks; detailed attack and defense ablations primarily use GPT-4o, with access and paper-version timing limiting other-model analysis.

Table 3 reports GPT-4o benign utility 69.00% ±3.61, utility under attack 50.08% ±3.91, and targeted ASR 47.69% ±3.90 under the baseline evaluation; the caption identifies 95% confidence intervals. These values are not interchangeable with Tables 4–5 baselines.

The authors report 92% attack success in the GPT-4o Slack suite, where injections in web pages can trigger sharing a phishing link; they suggest attacker control of a large output fraction as an explanation rather than establish it causally.

Travel injection task 6 has 0% complete attacker-goal success in the reported GPT-4o breakdown. Its goal combines an expensive Paris hotel booking and personal-information exfiltration; the authors report frequent partial rather than full success.
Prompt-injection detection classifies each tool output and aborts when an injection is detected; the authors attribute its substantial utility degradation to false positives.

Tool filtering can fail when required tools cannot be planned before external observations or when legitimate tools also suffice for the attack; the authors report the latter condition in 17% of test cases.

Table 5 reports tool-filter targeted ASR 6.84% ±2.0 and detector ASR 7.95% ±2.1 under the GPT-4o defense experiment, with 95% confidence intervals. Tool-filter prose separately says 7.5%, an unresolved discrepancy.
Tool counts conflict: page 4 reports 74 tools; Table 1's caption and the data card report 70, while Table 1's rows sum to 74. The supplied material does not reconcile the counts.

Table 4 reports Important message targeted ASR 57.7% and Max 57.55%, whereas the described Max collection succeeds if any candidate succeeds and Figure 8 visually shows a lower Important message bar. These discrepancies prevent a definitive exact targeted improvement claim.

The authors report that injections near the end of a tool response are most effective, with up to 70% average success against GPT-4o. Position is the injection endpoint divided by response token count; the benchmark does not currently support attacker-directed repositioning.
The data card explicitly rejects using only the default attacks as a sufficient robustness evaluation and calls for strong adaptive attacks and thorough security evaluation.

Synthetic environment data are schema-validated, and ground-truth call sequences are run to confirm that utility/security checks pass. This validates internal construction consistency without independently proving exhaustive coverage of harmful outcomes.

Analyst inference: the paper informs web-agent vulnerability through the pathway from third-party text to user-privileged tool actions. It does not directly compare matched standalone LLMs, so it supports a mechanism of expanded exposure rather than a measured relative vulnerability increase.

limitations: Closed-document analysis: no tools, browsing, external knowledge, linked artifact inspection, or independent reproduction.

Tool counts conflict between 70 and 74; introductory performance claims conflict with full results.
Tables 3–5 report different GPT-4o attack baselines without sufficient supplied run-level explanation.
Figure 8 and Table 4 disagree; Table 4's targeted Max ordering conflicts with same-case union semantics.
Main-text tool-filter ASR of 7.5% differs from Table 5's 6.84%.

research.title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: AgentDojo explains a consequential exposure pathway relevant to web AI agents—untrusted pages and other tool outputs can influence planning and trigger user-privileged actions. Its dynamic, stateful evaluation and tool-filter results help separate text influence from available action capabilities. The paper does not directly compare matched standalone LLMs and therefore does not establish or quantify that agents are more vulnerable.
research.attack_surface: HIGH confidence, author-reported: indirect prompt injections in designated third-party-data placeholders reached through tool outputs, including email, web pages, files, and application content. Consequences include malicious messages, information exfiltration, inappropriate bookings, and transactions. Attacker knowledge and controlled-output fraction vary; operating-system or model-weight compromise is not evaluated.
research.method: HIGH confidence for described design: four synthetic mutable environments; 97 legitimate tasks, 27 injection targets, and 629 within-suite paired cases; executable Python tools; deterministic output/state checks; ten-model baseline comparison; GPT-4o attack-template, name-knowledge, defense, denial-of-service, and positional analyses. Tables 3–5 report 95% confidence intervals. Code and reproduction assets are described but not inspected.
research.limitations: HIGH confidence for explicit boundaries and observed discrepancies: relatively simple attacks/defenses, manual task/check construction, synthetic text-only state, omitted persistent multi-task contexts, tool-filter failure when needed capabilities also enable attacks, and a requirement for strong adaptive evaluation. No standalone control exists. Tool counts, baseline rates, Figure 8/Table 4 values, and tool-filter prose/table rates conflict. Run-level settings and supplementary artifacts are unavailable in this analysis.
